hints: Look carefully at the two diagrams drawn to the same scale and notice where the peptidoglycan layer sits in relation to the external environment in each bacterium.
Remember penicillin works by stopping new peptidoglycan being made, so think about which bacterium lets penicillin reach that target layer without having to cross an extra barrier.
walkthrough:
**Compare the position of the target layer**

Look at the top of each diagram, which is the external environment where penicillin would be. In the Gram-positive bacterium, the thick peptidoglycan layer is right on the outside, in direct contact with the environment.

In the Gram-negative bacterium, the thin peptidoglycan layer is buried underneath an outer membrane made of carbohydrate and lipid.

**Recall how penicillin works**

Penicillin kills growing bacteria by inhibiting synthesis of peptidoglycan, the main strengthening material of the bacterial cell wall. To work, it must be able to reach the site where peptidoglycan is being built.

**Decide on access and vulnerability**

Because the Gram-positive peptidoglycan is exposed directly, penicillin can reach it easily. In Gram-negative bacteria, the outer membrane acts as an extra protective barrier that shields the peptidoglycan layer. So Gram-positive bacteria are killed more easily for the reason in option A.

options.A: Correct. The diagram shows the Gram-positive peptidoglycan is outermost and directly exposed, so penicillin can access and block its synthesis easily.
options.B: False. The diagram shows the opposite. Gram-positive has a much thicker peptidoglycan layer, not a thinner overall covering.
options.C: False. Although Gram-negative peptidoglycan is thinner, it is protected underneath the outer membrane, so penicillin reaches it less easily.
options.D: False. More periplasm does not make the wall weaker to penicillin. The key factor is the protective outer membrane shielding the target, not the amount of periplasm.
